outline.chapter_title: Case Background, Technology, and Procedural Posture
outline.description: Introduces the parties, the accused PIM-cancellation feature in Nokia radios used by AT&T, the patents-in-suit, and the trial outcome that set up the appeal. Provides essential technical context on intermodulation products (IMPs) and passive intermodulation (PIM) needed to follow the court’s analysis.
subtopics: Parties and accused products: AT&T and Nokia’s PIM-C feature in Nokia radios
Technical backdrop: IMPs and PIM, internal vs. external PIM, and why radios care
Asserted claims: ’134 patent (method isolating signals and canceling IMPs); ’775 patent (generating cancellation signals via specified multiplications)
District court proceedings: jury verdict of validity and infringement; lump-sum damages of $166,303,391
Post-trial motions: JMOLs and new-trial motions denied
Appeal posture and jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)

outline.chapter_title: Standards of Review and Claim-Construction Framework
outline.description: Sets out the governing appellate standards and the specific claim-construction rulings that frame the infringement analyses, explaining how they steer the Federal Circuit’s review of the jury verdict and JMOL denials.
subtopics: JMOL standard (regional circuit/Fifth Circuit): de novo; evidence must overwhelmingly favor movant to overturn
Substantial-evidence review of jury infringement findings: could a reasonable jury find for the verdict winner?
Claim construction: de novo review; underlying factual findings for clear error
Construction specific to ’775 patent: “three signals S1, S2 and S3” are separately identifiable, not necessarily unique
Prosecution history and scope: no clear and unambiguous disavowal limiting claims to systems with three unique input signals
Preservation and waiver context: district court deemed “uniqueness” argument waived at Rule 50(a), but Federal Circuit addressed merits of scope and focused decision on evidentiary insufficiency

outline.chapter_title: The ’134 Patent—Sampling Limitation and Expert Testimony Breakdown
outline.description: Explains why the Federal Circuit held the evidence insufficient on the ’134 patent’s key sampling requirement, focusing on the mapping of claimed signals to the accused architecture and the expert’s contradictory testimony.
subtopics: Key limitation 1[a]: receiver must sample a passband containing both “signals of interest” and “interference generating signals” to create a bit stream
Finesse’s proof theory: Nokia diagram; RF ADC as the sampler; mapping “signals of interest” to DL(TX) reference and “interference generating signals” to the modeled PIM path
Temporal/architectural mismatch: modeled PIM path is generated downstream (e.g., in FPGA) after the RF ADC; cannot be sampled before it exists
Cross-examination pivot: reference to x1 and x2 without clearly mapping them to the claimed “signals of interest” and “interference generating signals”
District court’s JMOL denial: inferred that x1/x2 were the claimed signals despite expert’s repeated identification of DL(TX) and modeled PIM path

Federal Circuit’s reasoning: testimony confusing and self-contradictory; no clear mapping; reliance on Johns Hopkins v. Datascope regarding insufficiency when an expert’s contradictory testimony underpins the verdict
Result: no substantial evidence supports limitation 1[a]; reversal of JMOL denial as to all asserted ’134 claims

outline.chapter_title: The ’775 Patent—Failure to Prove Seven Required Multiplications from Three Signals
outline.description: Analyzes the ’775 patent’s requirement to generate IMP cancellation signals via seven specified third-order multiplications of three signals, and details why the trial record did not substantiate that the accused radios perform all seven.
subtopics: Claim 1 structure: co-located transmitter/receiver; passive IMPs; ICS generation “continuously and near real time” using copies of transmitter signals
Critical limitation 1[d]: generate an n-th order ICS by seven third-order products of S1, S2, S3 (explicitly enumerated)
Claim-construction backdrop: “three signals” need only be separately identifiable; not limited to three unique signals; no disavowal of two-unique-signal systems
Finesse’s trial proof: reliance on Nokia document showing three distinct multiplications (e.g., x1·|x1|·|x1|, x1·x1·x2', x1·|x2|·|x2|) and operations involving modulus and complex conjugates
Gap in proof: document and testimony identify only three distinct multiplications; no evidence of repetitions to reach seven; no trial mapping tying the three to the seven enumerated products
Appellate attempts to supply mappings and point to a set of ten multiplications in the documents could not cure the trial-record deficiency
Result: no reasonable jury could find all seven claimed multiplications; reversal of JMOL denial as to all asserted ’775 claims

outline.description: Concludes with the consequences of the noninfringement rulings and practical lessons for litigating complex signal-processing patents and expert-driven infringement theories.
subtopics: Damages award: $166,303,391 lump-sum for life of ’134 and ’775; district court denied JMOL and new trial
Disposition: reversal of JMOL denials on noninfringement for both patents; damages award vacated
No need to reach new-trial-on-damages arguments in light of noninfringement

Key lessons: precise, consistent expert mappings to claim elements; respecting signal flow and timing (sampling cannot precede signal generation); ensuring documentary evidence matches claim operations (literal multiplications vs. modulus/complex conjugate); cannot rely on appellate clarifications to fill trial-record gaps
